idiom_name: mutex-guarded registry of per-subscriber channels + publish fan-out loop
implementation_notes: A Go channel delivers each value to exactly one receiver, so it is a point-to-point primitive: broadcast requires a hand-written fan-out - a mutex-guarded set of per-subscriber channels (or a snapshot of it) that the publisher iterates, sending each subscriber its own copy, with a buffer size per subscriber as the overflow contract. The pipeline idiom that reads one channel from many goroutines is the opposite semantic (work sharing / competing consumers), and closing a channel is a broadcast shutdown signal, not a message. Registries of this size are usually kept explicit rather than hidden behind a library.
pitfalls: Sending on a subscriber's channel while holding the registry lock lets one slow subscriber block the publisher and every peer; buffer per subscriber and decide drop/disconnect policy in the default case.
Closing a channel twice, or closing while a sender may still send, panics; only the subscriber (or a separate done channel) may own close.
An unbuffered send inside Publish turns the broadcast into a rendezvous with the slowest consumer.
Range over a channel stops at close, not at cancellation; subscribers need a done/context arm in their select.
